[h3] 8.5 / 10[/h3] 

A rather simple game / typing simulator for people enjoying solving rather simple but engaging puzzles.

You play trough a story and receive missions to hack computers using different tools and commands. It's not really a representation of IRL hacking but it also doesn't really try to be. Most missions are very cozy and chill and there are only a few 'stressful' missions. The story is nothing special but it somehow keeps you engaged. 

I think it scratched an itch I din't know I had - to look trough other people's files and just being curious of what I can find in the next mission. It has some little secrets here and there too so a lot of times it feels rewarding to check everything out thoroughly. The IRC logs are quite cringe though LOL!

The difficulty is not very high and typing the commands is quite repetitive but it didn't really matter, I still very much enjoyed it.

Things I would improve:

- The Netmap which shows all the known servers as nodes gets quite annnoying in mid and late game because there are too many servers to memorize their positions and sometimes it costs more time than it should to pick the right node
- Having multiple savestates of the same playtrough would be nice since you can hardlock yourself or miss story branches and have to start over again to reach them
- A few optional hardcore puzzles would have been nice to make the game a little more challenging if you want to
- QoL improvements

Overall a very niche but enjoyable game.

BUY THIS GAME!!! YOU WILL NOT REGRET IT!!! BUY THIS *AND* THE LABYRINTHS DLC!!!

I would hardly call this a game as it is more of an experience and a ABSOLUTELY AMAZING ONE at that!

Listen... you are going to start out knowing NOTHING. Over time, you will learn how to navigate systems and implement your tools to get into systems. But there is SO MUCH MORE to this game than that! You start to intuit how things work and what to do, even when no one is holding your hand and spoon-feeding you directions. You will make discoveries and piece together stories and relationships. You start digging on your own with NO ONE telling you to. There are moments where you are going to be STRESSED OUT! LOL It's absolutely wonderful how immersed you get in this work of art.

Remember in Skyrim, where if you read the books that you find, even if they don't trigger a quest, they actually HAVE quests in them? Remember how awesome it felt to figure it out all on your own and reap the rewards of your mental efforts? THIS GAME is like that ALL THE TIME!!!

I will admit... there were parts of this game where my eyes teared up, partly because I realized what was going on, partly because I realized what I was capable of, and partly because there wasn't more when I beat the game... but there IS more: Extensions.

HackNet Extensions allows YOU, the player, to design and build your OWN missions/quests and share them! Now YOU can be the one to create experiences for OTHERS to have.

This game... is one of the COOLEST games I have EVER played. If you don't buy it, you are robbing yourself and missing out on something AWESOME.


[ TO THE CREATOR/MAKERS OF THE GAME:

I want to say: Thank you SO much for this experience. I am very appreciative and amazed at your work. I also want to apologize for not getting my hands on your work sooner. I am REALLY looking forward to crafting my OWN HackNet Extension; I think I have some pretty cool ideas. :D

I’ve got Hacknet as a gift when I was learning UNIX commands and then bash scripting for work, what probably made me a perfect target player. It got me really hooked on the Linux system, and I found it a great introduction to coding as a whole. 

That said, it’s not a complicated game and no previous coding knowledge is required to play it. The "real" part mostly involves file manipulations and basic SSH usage, while the hacking part  is based on running non-real programs to break into chosen devices and perform said manipulations.

The whole game takes place in an artificial Linux environment that can be modified to a certain degree. It makes the title even more immersive and believable.

However, it’s worth noting that the core gameplay can become a little repetitive after a few hours, not to say "grindy". It’s definitely not for everyone, but the 2-hour refund window is more than enough to determine if it suits you.

A fun game that makes you feel like a hacker. 

The internal logic of the game is really good, and the game does offer some possibility of mastery.

The pacing is actually EXCELLENT and something that a lot of games like this get wrong: it teaches the player the mechanics and scales up the difficulty in a really nice way. 

For people unfamiliar with computers and UNIX systems, this is a great entryway into learning the basics of navigation, and also mimics some of the conceptual problemsolving skills one needs to be a hacker.

There were times that I was overthinking problems, and most of the time the game simply requires you to "search and find the answer" rather than figure out a more complex sollution, though there are a couple of paths in the game that allows you to flex your skills and challenges you if you're up to it.

The story and writing is trying to punch above its weight but it serves its purpose. Sometimes it got a chuckle out of me, and it was fun to dig through files and find some silly conversations. But its a tad cliche, even for 2013. The plot allows you to live out the fantasy within the limitations and rules of the game mechanics, so its effective but not groundbreaking.

Overall the best OS-simulator "hacker" game I've played so far.

An interesting puzzle game that takes place mostly inside of a command-line interface. The story for this game isn't anything special, it's a linear adventure as you knock out hacking missions (one optional) in order to solve the overarching mystery regarding a deceased hacker.

Now, this game is NOT real hacking by any means (although it does make use of problem solving skills that are used in real-world offensive hacking), unless you count being a script kiddie that found the 7 dragon balls of computer programming, capable of breaching corporate networks and cracking SSH encryption with a command like "PortHack 22". That being said, you don't need any major computational knowledge to play the game, it's a learn as you go experience, and you might actually learn some basics about computer networking like IP addresses and ports.

Although I played this game a while ago, the gameplay did stick with me and it was good enough to earn a recommendation from me. Also has a cool LVL 5 trading card badge that I rep on my profile. If you're interested in computers or cybersec and want an afternoon to kill, this might just be the game for you.

Hacknet is a unique and immersive hacking simulator that manages to blend educational elements with engaging gameplay to deliver an experience that feels both authentic and accessible. Developed by Team Fractal Alligator, the game places players in the role of a recently deceased hacker whose death was mysteriously logged in the system, prompting you to follow their digital footsteps through a series of hacking tasks. From the moment you begin, Hacknet pulls you into a gritty, text-based cyber world that relies heavily on realistic command-line interfaces, compelling storytelling, and a sense of discovery that is rarely found in traditional puzzle or adventure games.

At its core, Hacknet is all about learning and using real-world hacking concepts in a fictional setting. The gameplay revolves around typing actual Unix-based commands, running scripts, cracking passwords, and exploiting network vulnerabilities. Unlike many games that simplify hacking into a series of quick minigames or button presses, Hacknet demands attention to detail and encourages experimentation. The command line interface is intuitive yet detailed, and the game introduces commands gradually, allowing players to build a solid understanding of the mechanics as they progress. The pacing strikes a perfect balance between tutorialization and challenge, making it approachable for newcomers without feeling watered down for those with some technical knowledge.

The narrative is one of the standout features of Hacknet. It unfolds through in-game emails, chat logs, and system messages, painting a picture of a shadowy digital underworld filled with intrigue, moral ambiguity, and complex characters. You’re not just hacking for the sake of hacking; there is an overarching mystery and a compelling story that motivates your actions. The writing is sharp, immersive, and at times surprisingly emotional, which elevates the experience beyond a purely mechanical simulation. The game’s episodic structure ensures that the story unfolds organically, revealing new layers and twists as you delve deeper into the cyber realm.

Visually, Hacknet embraces a minimalist aesthetic that perfectly suits its subject matter. The black terminal screen with green and white text, simple window layouts, and sparse but effective use of icons and alerts all contribute to a tense, focused atmosphere. This stark visual style keeps distractions at bay and mirrors the real-world hacking environment, which is often devoid of flashy graphics or unnecessary clutter. Sound design is subtle but impactful—the ambient electronic soundtrack and occasional notification sounds create a sense of urgency and immersion without overwhelming the player.

One of the game’s greatest strengths lies in its open-ended approach to problem-solving. While certain missions have specific goals, there are often multiple ways to achieve them, encouraging players to think creatively and strategically. Tools can be upgraded and customized, and players must learn to manage limited resources like access time and software capabilities. This encourages careful planning and prioritization, and often rewards lateral thinking and patience. The inclusion of realistic constraints, such as the risk of being traced or locked out, adds tension and stakes to each hacking attempt.

The community surrounding Hacknet has also contributed significantly to its longevity. The game supports modding, and players have created custom missions, alternate storylines, and new tools that expand the gameplay experience far beyond the base game. This openness to user-generated content keeps the game fresh and provides a platform for those interested in exploring hacking concepts in even more depth.

While Hacknet is highly praised, it’s important to note that its appeal is somewhat niche. Players looking for fast-paced action or high-octane thrills might find the methodical, text-heavy gameplay slow or dense. The learning curve, though well-managed, can be steep for those unfamiliar with command-line interfaces or hacking terminology. However, for players fascinated by computers, cybersecurity, or puzzle-solving, Hacknet offers a deeply satisfying and often enlightening experience that feels genuinely rewarding.

In conclusion, Hacknet stands out as a rare title that successfully combines educational value with compelling storytelling and engaging gameplay mechanics. Its realistic portrayal of hacking, grounded in authentic command-line use, sets it apart from other cyber-themed games that often rely on gimmicks or unrealistic portrayals. The game’s narrative depth, minimalist yet effective presentation, and open-ended problem-solving create an experience that is both intellectually stimulating and highly entertaining. For anyone curious about the world of hacking or simply looking for a unique puzzle-adventure game, Hacknet is a must-play that continues to impress years after its release.
